title: What's Under My Carpet? Refinishing the Hardwood Hiding in Kirkland Homes
meta: Many Kirkland homes built before 1980 have oak under the carpet. Wills Flooring shows how to check, what to expect and what refinishing costs per sq ft.
keywords: hardwood under carpet Kirkland, how to tell if there is hardwood under carpet, refinish hardwood floors under carpet cost, pulling up carpet to find hardwood, oak floors under carpet 1960s house, Kirkland hardwood floor refinishing

blocks.lead: If your Kirkland house was built before about 1980, there is a good chance the carpet in the living room, hallway and bedrooms is hiding oak strip flooring that can be sanded and refinished for $3.99 per sq ft.
blocks.detail: Houghton, Juanita and Rose Hill ramblers from the 1950s and 60s almost always have it. Split-levels from the 70s usually do on the main floor. Newer Finn Hill and Bridle Trails homes often have oak in the entry only, with plywood everywhere else.

blocks.html: Every spring a few Kirkland buyers send us the same photo: a corner of beige carpet folded back in a bedroom closet, and under it, honey-colored oak strips with a row of staples. The question is whether the whole house looks like that, how bad the wood is, and whether refinishing it beats new flooring. Here is how to find out before you spend a Saturday pulling carpet, what we typically find under it in each Kirkland neighborhood, and what the refinishing actually costs.

blocks.text: How to check without wrecking the carpet

items.text: Pull the carpet off the tack strip in a closet corner with pliers. It hooks back on afterward. You are looking for wood strips with a visible grain running one direction, usually 2 1/4 in wide, not sheets of plywood with a rough face.

Lift a heat register and look at the edge of the floor around the duct. You can see the thickness of the wood and whether it is solid strip or plywood, and this spot tells us how many sandings the floor has left.
items.note: 3/4 in solid strip has plenty of life. Anything under 1/2 in needs a careful look.

items.text: If the top stair has a rounded wood nosing under the carpet edge, the upstairs hall is probably wood too. A square plywood edge usually means carpet was original there.

Kirkland builders in the 60s and 70s often put oak in living areas and bedrooms but plywood or particleboard in kitchens, baths and family room additions. One closet does not tell you about the whole house.

blocks.text: What condition to expect, and what refinishing fixes

items.title: Staples and tack strip holes
items.text: Thousands of pad staples and a row of nail holes at every wall. All of it comes out, and the holes sand or fill away. This is the normal state of carpeted oak and it is not damage.

items.title: Pet stains
items.text: Dark or black blotches where a pet went repeatedly, often in a bedroom corner. Surface stains sand out. Stains that soaked deep may stay as a shadow or need board replacement. We tell you which at the estimate, not after sanding.

items.title: Uneven color
items.text: The wood under the carpet is lighter than the wood that was exposed in the entry or under a rug edge. Sanding takes both back to bare wood so the color evens out. It is one reason a recoat is almost never possible on a floor coming out from under carpet.

items.title: Water marks and cupping
items.text: Gray rings under a plant stand or darkened boards near a slider. Light marks sand out. Cupped boards from a long-term leak may flatten after drying or may need replacing. Kirkland lakefront homes see this more than the hills do.

blocks.text: Refinish the oak or replace it? A Rose Hill example

blocks.html: A 1972 split-level with 780 sq ft of oak on the main floor plus a 13-tread staircase. Refinishing, natural finish: 780 × $3.99 + 13 × $55 = $3,112 + $715 = $3,827. With a stain to take the orange out: 780 × $6.50 + 13 × $75 = $5,070 + $975 = $6,045. Installing new engineered hardwood over the same area is $3.25 per sq ft in labor, plus the material, plus $125 per stair, and you throw away 50-year-old solid oak to do it. When the wood is sound, refinishing wins on price and on what Kirkland buyers expect to see in a listing.

a.title: When the oak is worth keeping
items: Solid strip at least 1/2 in thick at the register
Stains and scratches are surface deep
Boards are flat, tight and not spongy
You like oak, natural or stained; it takes stain well

b.title: When it is not
items: Particleboard or plywood, not wood strip
Wide black urine stains through the boards in several rooms
Cupping, soft spots or a floor that moves underfoot
Two or three earlier sandings have left it thin

blocks.title: Do not pull all the carpet before we see it:
blocks.text: Leave the carpet down until the estimate. It protects the wood, it lets us see the stains before you scrub them, and we include tear-out and staple removal in the quote. A weekend of pulling staples with a screwdriver is not a savings worth having.
Getting the best result from a floor that has been hidden for decades

items.html: Check the thickness before you commit. The register trick tells us whether the floor can take a full sanding. Most Kirkland oak from the 50s to 70s has been sanded once or never.

Decide on color with samples on your floor. Red oak from 1965 is orange under a natural finish. A stain at $6.50 per sq ft can take it light and neutral, which is what most Eastside buyers want. We put sample stains on your actual floor after sanding.

Plan the kitchen and family room now. If they were never wood, new flooring there has to meet the refinished oak at a doorway. Matching new hardwood is possible; a clean transition to vinyl plank is the budget route.
Add dust containment in an occupied house. Our sanders are vacuum-connected, and the $250 sealing and air scrubber option makes the difference when you live there through the job.

faq.q: How can I tell if there is hardwood under my carpet?
faq.a: Pull back a corner in a closet with pliers and look for narrow wood strips with grain running one way. Then lift a floor register to see the edge and thickness of the floor. Wood strip about 2 1/4 in wide and 3/4 in thick is refinishable solid oak. Rough sheets are plywood or particleboard.

faq.q: How much does it cost to refinish hardwood floors found under carpet?
faq.a: Wills Flooring charges $3.99 per sq ft for a full sand and natural finish, or $6.50 with stain, with a 500 sq ft minimum. Stairs are $55 to $75 per tread. Carpet tear-out, staple removal and any board replacement are quoted at the free estimate. A typical 800 sq ft Kirkland main floor is about $3,200 natural.

faq.q: Can floors that were under carpet just be recoated instead of sanded?
faq.a: Almost never. The wood under the carpet is a different color from any exposed areas, it has staple holes and pad residue, and the old finish is usually worn or contaminated. A full sanding is what evens the color and removes the marks. Recoating is for floors with an intact finish.

faq.q: Will the staple holes and tack strip holes show after refinishing?
faq.a: No. Pad staples leave tiny holes that disappear with sanding, and the tack strip nail holes along the walls are filled and sit under the baseboard shadow line. The only marks that can remain are deep pet stains or water damage, and we point those out before we start.

faq.q: What if I find particleboard instead of hardwood?
faq.a: Particleboard was a common carpet underlayment in Kirkland homes from the late 1970s and 80s. It cannot be sanded or finished. The choices are to cover it with vinyl plank or laminate, or to remove it and install new hardwood on the plywood subfloor beneath. We price both at the estimate.
